newsitem.title: CHINA: Thai baht seen under pressure as confidence wanes.
newsitem.headline: Thai baht seen under pressure as confidence wanes.

text.p: Confidence has hit an all-time low in Thailand's ability to manage its worst economic crisis in at least a decade, and the baht remained vulnerable, fund managers said on Friday.
"There is not much confidence that Thailand has got its act together, which is why the baht is still under pressure," said Daniel Hemmant, currency fund manager at Guinness Flight Asia.
"It's pretty hard to be convinced they've got any sort of handle on the situation. Things are deteriorating, but they're objecting to (International Monetary Fund) involvement."

Until Thailand comes forward with a credible package to deal with its problems, the Thai baht will confront more speculation and other Southeast Asian currencies can expect to get hit in the crossfire, Hemmant said.

Thai Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya said he will announce an economic package within two weeks that would help stabilise the baht, which has slumped 25 percent since speculators forced a de facto devaluation on July 2.
The pressure is mounting on Thailand. The baht fell to a record low of 32.70 against the U.S. dollar on Thursday.

Moody's Investors Service Inc has described Thailand's outlook as "uncertain" and said it would monitor Thailand's policy reforms closely to ensure they are appropriate and reflect the country's A3 foreign currency rating.

George Leung, economic adviser at Hongkong and Shanghai Bank, confirmed that the currency situation was still unstable, even though markets seemed generally quiet on Friday and hedging accounted for most of the activity.

"The situation hasn't been settled yet. We need to check out how the Thai government will react further to this situation, and whether speculators will shift their focus to other countries," he said. "(IMF involvement) all depends on whether there will be another round of attack."

Hemmant said another round of speculation on the baht was certainly possible. The central bank's refusal this week to lift capital controls to allow inflows that would cut interest rates failed to impress investors, he said.
Thailand would have difficulty dealing with further depreciation of the baht, Leung said.

"Change is deemed to be necessary, but it is a matter of process," he said. "A short-term sharp devaluation by speculators will bring greater pain in the short-term before benefits can be realised longer-term."

Other Asian nations remain at risk of further contagion, partly because poor disclosure in some of these Southeast Asian nations prevented them from effectively disputing economic parallels with Thailand.
"Obviously Thailand is a worse case scenario, but other economies have the potential to resemble a number of problems in Thailand," said Hemmant.
"We get assurances that lending is under control, but Thailand said that, too, and the difficulty is that the levels of disclosure aren't good enough to feel comfortable."
The obvious parallels are current account deficits and overheating economies, with financial sectors heavily exposed to an inflated property sector, he said.
